protocol.name: gex_menu_v1

description.summary: a program's menus, presented by the compositor's shell

protocol.description:
A program with a menu bar -- a Mac application's main menu, a GTK or Qt application's exported menus, a Win32 window's HMENU -- can hand the menu's description to the compositor instead of drawing it inside its window. The shell then presents it by its own conventions: a global menu bar at the top of the screen, a strip in the frame it draws round the window, a button that opens it. The program keeps the menu's meaning: it says what the items are, brings them up to date when one of its menus is about to be shown, and acts when the shell says an item was chosen.
Negotiation is by the global's presence. A compositor advertises gex_menu_manager_v1 only when its shell presents menus; a client that sees it publishes its menus and draws no menu bar of its own, and one that does not sees and does everything as before. A client's context menus, pop-up buttons and other menus it opens itself are not part of this: they stay its own windows (xdg_popup).
The model
A gex_menu_v1 object is one tree. Its nodes are items, each named by a number the client chooses, unique within the tree and opaque to the compositor (zero is not an item: it names the tree's root, the menu bar itself). An item with the submenu flag is also a menu: its children are the items shown when it opens, and where a request or event takes a "menu" it is that item's number, or zero for the root. A number keeps meaning the same item for as long as the client goes on describing it, so a shell can keep a menu open across updates, and remember an item to activate from a shortcut of its own.
A tree belongs either to the whole client -- an application's menu bar, shown while any of the client's toplevels has the keyboard; or the menu a shell shows for the application's icon in its dock or taskbar -- or to one toplevel (a window that has a menu bar of its own). The menu for a window is its own tree if it has one, else its client's menu bar tree.
State is double-buffered. The requests that describe items (item, the item_* requests, set_items, remove_item, set_title) accumulate and take effect together at commit, so a shell never sees half an update. The first commit publishes the tree; later ones change it, and a client sends only what changed. Nothing a client describes is lost by not being mentioned again: an item keeps its properties and a menu its children until the client sets them anew or removes the item.
Liveness
Programs keep their menus lazily: whether Undo is enabled, what its title is, which documents the Window menu lists, is worked out when the menu is about to be seen. So before a shell shows a menu it sends about_to_open, and the client brings that menu's items up to date (item requests and a commit, if anything changed) and answers ack_open with the event's serial. A shell should show the menu on the ack, and may show the state it already has if the ack is slow in coming (a program that is busy must not make the menu bar dead), correcting it when the commit arrives. A menu the shell stops showing is closed. about_to_open for the root asks for the bar's own items (the titles along it) to be made current, and is not required before showing the bar.
A client may commit changes at any time, with no menu open: a document's new name, a check mark that moved. A shell showing the tree redraws.
Choosing an item is activate, with the modifiers held. The client does what it does when the item is chosen in its own menu -- including nothing, when the item turns out to be disabled: the client's own state decides, not the shell's copy of it. activate needs no about_to_open before it, so a shell may run an item from a shortcut it owns (it reads the item's shortcut from the tree, or assigns its own). The shortcuts a client describes stay the client's business while one of its surfaces has the keyboard: the keys reach it as wl_keyboard events as they always did and it acts on them itself. They are described so that a shell can draw them beside the items, and so that it can offer them when the client does not have the keyboard, if its conventions want that.
Neutrality
Nothing here belongs to one toolkit. Shortcuts are a key named as the W3C UI Events "key" values name keys, with a mask of the four modifiers every keymap has. Roles are optional hints from a fixed vocabulary of lower-case words, there so a shell can find the items its conventions place specially (an application menu, Quit, Preferences, a Window or Help menu); a client that knows none sets none, and a shell ignores the ones it does not know.

interface.name: gex_menu_manager_v1
interface.description: The global. Advertised only by a compositor whose shell presents menus; see the protocol's description.

entry.name: role_taken
entry.summary: the client already has an application menu of this kind

entry.name: surface_taken
entry.summary: the surface already has a menu

entry.name: bad_kind
entry.summary: not a kind of application menu this version knows

enum.name: kind

description.summary: what an application menu is for

enum.description: Which of a client's menus a tree is.

entry.name: menu_bar
entry.description: The menus shown while any of the client's toplevels has the keyboard, unless that toplevel has a menu of its own. Its root's children are the bar's titles, each a submenu.

entry.name: dock

description.summary: the application's dock or taskbar menu

entry.description: Items a shell adds to the menu it shows for the application's icon or task button. Its root's children are those items.

request.name: get_application_menu

description.summary: a menu that belongs to the whole client

request.description: Makes the client's tree of the given kind. A client has at most one of each kind at a time (role_taken otherwise); destroying it leaves the client free to make another.

request.name: get_surface_menu

description.summary: a menu that belongs to one toplevel

request.description: Makes the menu bar of one surface, which should be or become an xdg_toplevel. While that toplevel has the keyboard a shell shows this tree and not the client's application menu bar. A surface has at most one (surface_taken otherwise). The tree is gone from the shell when the surface is destroyed; the object stays, inert, until the client destroys it.

interface.name: gex_menu_v1
interface.description: See the protocol's description for the model. Requests other than commit, ack_open and destroy change pending state, applied by commit.

entry.name: bad_item
entry.summary: item number zero, or a number never described

entry.name: bad_tree
entry.summary: at commit, an item is in two menus, in itself, or a menu's child was never described

entry.name: bad_image
entry.summary: an image larger than allowed, or whose file is too short

entry.name: bad_serial
entry.summary: ack_open of a serial no about_to_open carried

description.summary: what kind of item, and how it is shown

entry.name: disabled
entry.summary: cannot be chosen; a shell draws it dimmed

entry.name: hidden
entry.summary: not shown at all, and takes no room

entry.name: separator
entry.summary: a dividing line; its title and the rest mean nothing

entry.name: submenu
entry.summary: opens a menu: its children, which may be none yet

entry.name: alternate

description.summary: stands in for the item before it

entry.description: The item replaces the nearest preceding item that is not an alternate, while exactly its shortcut's modifiers are held with the menu open (Close, and Close All with Alt held). A shell that does not present alternates treats the item as hidden.

entry.name: header
entry.summary: a label for the items after it; cannot be chosen

entry.name: mixed
entry.summary: true of part of what it applies to

enum.name: modifiers
enum.description: Named as the compositor's keymap names them, which is how wl_keyboard.modifiers reports them: Shift, Control, Mod1 and Mod4. Mod4 is the key a Mac keyboard labels Command, a PC keyboard with the Windows mark, and a shell usually calls Super or Meta; Mod1 is Alt, a Mac's Option.

entry.name: template
entry.description: Only the image's alpha means anything: a shell draws it in the colour of the item's text, as it would a glyph.

request.name: destroy
request.description: The shell stops showing it at once. Events already sent for it may be ignored.

request.name: set_title
request.description: For an application menu, the application's name as it should be shown to a person (a shell may title the application's own menu with it); for a surface's, whatever names the window's menu, or nothing. Pending state.

request.name: item
request.description:
Makes the item `id` if the tree has none, and sets what every item has: its flags, check mark, indentation (in levels, for an item shown as subordinate to the one above; zero for none) and title. The title is plain text, with no mnemonic marker. What the other item_* requests set is left as it was.
A new item is in no menu until a set_items names it. Zero is not an item (bad_item). Pending state.

request.name: item_shortcut

description.summary: the keys that choose an item

request.description:
`key` names the key as the W3C UI Events specification's KeyboardEvent "key" values do, for the unshifted key: one character for a key that types one, in lower case if it has case ("s", ",", "/", " " for the space bar), else the key's name ("Enter", "Tab", "Backspace", "Delete", "Escape", "ArrowUp", "ArrowDown", "ArrowLeft", "ArrowRight", "Home", "End", "PageUp", "PageDown", "F1" and so on). `modifiers` is every modifier held with it, Shift included: a shortcut a toolkit writes as a capital letter is the lower-case key with shift.
An empty key means the item has no shortcut, which is how one is taken away. Pending state.

request.name: item_role

description.summary: what an item is, for a shell that treats some specially

request.description:
A hint, one lower-case word from this list, or empty for none (which is what an item has until told otherwise). A shell may move, merge, retitle or restyle items by role; a client must not depend on it.
On a child of the menu bar's root: "application" (the menu of the application itself: About, Preferences, Quit; a Mac program's first menu), "file", "edit", "view", "window", "help".
On an item anywhere: "about", "preferences", "services" (a submenu of services other programs offer), "hide", "hide-others", "show-all", "quit", "new", "open", "close", "save", "print", "undo", "redo", "cut", "copy", "paste", "delete", "select-all", "minimize", "zoom", "fullscreen", "bring-all-to-front".
Later versions may add words; a shell ignores one it does not know. Pending state.

request.name: item_tooltip
request.description: A sentence a shell may show when the pointer rests on the item. Empty for none. Pending state.

request.name: item_image

description.summary: a small picture shown with an item

request.description:
The file holds width * height pixels from its start, rows top to bottom with no padding, each pixel 32 bits as wl_shm's argb8888 (alpha, red, green, blue from the most significant byte, in the machine's byte order; colour premultiplied by alpha). The picture is shown at width / scale by height / scale surface units, so a client with a 16-unit icon for a scale-2 output sends 32 by 32 and scale 2.
The compositor copies the pixels while it handles the request: the client may close and reuse the file as soon as it has sent it. No side may be longer than 128 pixels, and the file must hold them all (bad_image). Pending state.

request.name: remove_item
set_items
request.description: `items` is an array of 32-bit item numbers in the machine's byte order: the children of `menu` (an item with the submenu flag, or zero for the root), first to last. It replaces the menu's children whole; an item it leaves out is in no menu until named again. Pending state, checked at commit: every number must be a described item, and an item may be in one menu only and not inside itself (bad_tree).

request.name: commit
request.description: Everything pending takes effect together, and the shell shows the result. The first commit publishes the tree.

request.name: ack_open

description.summary: a menu about to open is up to date

request.description: Answers about_to_open: the menu's items are current as of the last commit. Sent after that commit, or alone if nothing needed changing. Acknowledging a serial acknowledges every earlier one.

event.name: about_to_open

description.summary: the shell is about to show a menu

event.description: The client makes the children of `menu` (zero: the root) current -- their titles, flags, check marks, and which there are -- commits if any changed, and sends ack_open with this serial. It need not make the menus below it current: each gets an event of its own when the shell opens it. The event may name an item the client has since removed, which the client acknowledges all the same.

event.name: closed

description.summary: the shell no longer shows a menu

event.description: Each about_to_open is paired with a closed, when the menu is put away or was never shown after all. Menus below it that were open are closed first.

event.name: activate
event.description: The client acts as it does when the item is chosen in a menu of its own, having checked for itself that the item can be chosen now. `modifiers` is what was held, for a program that looks. The client acts on the item named: a shell that presents alternates names the alternate when that is what it showed.
